adventure.title: The Cauldron of Nine Silences
adventure.synopsis: After Red Fen killed or scattered a third of the vale's field command, emergency work beneath Dunwarren's western gate opened the sealed chamber where King Branoc died. His oath-ring is the first true anchor recovered since his death—and the first chance to ask what he told Edric Taran before the gate closed. During the renewal feast, a crew must remove the Cauldron of Nine Silences or conduct Branoc's Full Asking before Lord Mael turns the households' memorial rolls into a Great Muster. Wax requires witnesses, kitchen bells open old roads, severed counsel guards the underkeep, and every escape ends in a dispute over who may keep what no one should own alone.
adventure.premise: Five weeks ago, Red Fen cost the vale a third of its field command. Masons underpinning Dunwarren's western gate against the next attack opened King Branoc's sealed command chamber. Efa Rill removed his oath-ring before Lord Mael closed the excavation. Branoc has never been summoned; the ring makes his first Full Asking possible. At dawn, the nobles renew the Gate Compact and House Taran's emergency powers in the name of his disputed command. At the fifth bell, Mael will chain the households' memorial rolls into a Great Muster and spend all nine silences for one military answer. Enter during the feast. Preserve ring and cauldron. Bring out the vessel or Branoc's whole witnessed answer before law hardens and the dead are diminished.
adventure.explanation:
The cauldron's proper rite is the Full Asking. A true anchor, the dead person's whole name, an honestly stated first question, free witnesses, and a named living keeper invite one honored dead person to return in recognition, memory, judgment, affection, refusal, reply, and will. The dead may answer, refuse, accuse, forgive, or ask what became of the people their answer once concerned. Free departure settles the nine silences back into relation for another generation.

Branoc has never been summoned. His body and intimate regalia vanished when Dunwarren nearly fell, and every surviving account of his final order descends from Edric Taran's recital. Red Fen forced Mael to underpin the western gate; the work exposed Branoc's sealed chamber. Efa Rill removed the oath-ring before Mael closed the excavation, and Gwyne Marr now holds it. The coalition's first question is exact: *What command did you give Edric Taran at the western gate?* They have promised to preserve the answer even if it condemns their cause.

The coalition offered chapel authentication under three witnesses: Brother Caddoc, Lady Aderyn's founder authority, and an opposed household jurist. Mael answered the emergency by annexing each safeguard: sole custody of the anchor, detention of the excavation foreman, searches of the masons' homes, and a royal claim over the witness bench itself. He does not hide what he wants. He makes every new danger an argument that one more key, keeper, witness, or dead voice must pass beneath his hand. Gwyne withheld the ring and notified Mere House because removal requires a keeper and destination. Mother Eluned rejected an immediate royal Asking before three hearths could convene and sent the Green Larks to recover the vessel. Their claim is rival custody, not a second commission.

For the dawn renewal, each household brought a memorial roll naming its honored service. Mael has chained those rolls into one war register and fitted copper combs to pass hundreds of names through separately opened bands. The resulting counsel may be accurate, but it loses the love, fear, promise, and duty that gave each answer proportion. Twelve earlier needle trials injured twelve dead and left narrow answers in the House of Borrowed Voices; they spent no whole silence and never called Branoc. The Great Muster will consume complete human faculties, then present the answer to the same nobles asked to renew Mael's authority.

Sabotage may delay the fifth bell while leaving ring, future Askings, and custody unresolved. The bronze vessel and living-oak cradle must travel together. Every consecrated threshold records keeper, destination, and authority. The Barrow Stair records exact declarations; the Borrowed Voices turn truth without purpose into security; the vault makes each threatened faculty visible; and the Reed Weir separates vessel, anchor, testimony, and keeper so that no single pursuer can erase every gain.

references.title: Gwyne Marr
references.summary: Outer-ward advocate and coalition broker who frames the heist, protects the exact question to Branoc, and refuses to let ancestry, possession, or desired outcomes outrun the surviving evidence.
references.content:
## What the record can bear

Gwyne Marr's mother's line descends from an outer-ward household stripped of land after the western gate closed. She has challenged House Taran's recital for twenty years, but refuses to use ancestry as a substitute for proof. She knows household rolls, oath forms, service roads, and the limits of each surviving source. The coalition's first question therefore remains exact and non-leading: *What command did you give Edric Taran at the western gate?*

## The coalition and the exact question

Gwyne speaks for descendants of the excluded households, two jurists, an abbot formerly connected to the cauldron's rites, and Lady Aderyn's deniable support. They seek to preserve the cauldron, conduct Branoc's first Full Asking, and preserve the whole answer even if it defeats their charge. Their earlier offer was a chapel inspection under Brother Caddoc, Aderyn's founder authority, and an opposed household jurist; Gwyne withdrew the anchor when Mael required sole emergency custody.

## What she cannot prove

Gwyne can commission agents, provide payment, records, routes, witnesses, and a publication commitment. Efa Rill's account, the oath-name, wax flaw, wear, and gate mortar let her establish an evidentiary chain for the ring without proving Branoc's command. Gwyne commands no present defense and cannot serve as military surety, settle the Nine Hearth Trust's claim, or turn escape into lawful custody without a named keeper and destination. Her present possession, allies, and negotiated terms remain matters for play.

references.title: Lord Mael Taran
references.summary: Lord of Dunwarren and bearer of House Taran's inherited emergency regime, using Red Fen's real military crisis to renew the Gate Compact, centralize custody, and conduct the Great Muster.
references.content:
## The warrant he inherits

Lord Mael Taran exercises House Taran's inherited emergency powers from Dunwarren. The doctrine descends from Edric Taran's recital of Branoc's western-gate command and has long justified control of roads, grain, levies, noble wards, and the cauldron whenever danger is declared. Red Fen makes the present danger real: the vale has lost a third of its field command and the northern road remains exposed.

## Every key beneath one command

Mael wants a defended vale, renewal of the Gate Compact, completion of the Great Muster, and continued Taran custody of the cauldron. He describes coerced counsel as inherited service and treats every new danger as reason to place another key, witness, keeper, wagon, or dead voice beneath one command. He nevertheless listens for an executable replacement: named offices, resources, keys, countersignatures, expiry, and a defense order that survives until morning.

## What survives until morning

Mael can direct Dunwarren's household resources and invoke the existing emergency regime, but neither Edric's recital, Branoc's oath-ring, the memorial rolls, borrowed answers, nor physical possession proves present royal title or unlimited ritual authority. Brother Caddoc keeps the rite, Aderyn holds founder authority, Vane's military orders remain bounded, and the dead retain refusal and reply. Mael may accept a constrained role, but only the office, override, custody share, and duration actually granted by a living covenant belong to him. Current custody, guard loyalty, bell state, and bargain terms remain matters for play.

references.title: King Branoc
references.summary: The dead king of the western-gate crisis, newly reachable through his oath-ring for a first Full Asking whose testimony can correct the inherited recital but cannot govern the changed present.
references.content:
## The man beneath the gate

King Branoc died during the western-gate crisis in the command chamber later sealed beneath Dunwarren. His body and intimate regalia were believed lost, and he has never been summoned. The recovered oath-ring bears his private oath-name, royal wax flaw, bodily wear, and chamber mortar. Those features can authenticate Branoc as the person invited; they do not establish what he commanded or grant authority to the ring's holder.

## The king may answer or refuse

The agreed first question is: *What command did you give Edric Taran at the western gate?* A proper Full Asking invites rather than compels. Branoc may answer, refuse, accuse, qualify, admit uncertainty, or ask what became of the people his answer concerned. His questions, conditions, uncertainty, and voluntary departure are part of the testimony and must not be abridged into a convenient royal ruling.

## What the dead king cannot command

Branoc's command was: “Bar the great leaves against the riders. Keep the wicket and the river stair until the outer ward is within. If the wall cannot hold, leave Dunwarren and save the people. A fort is a vessel; the realm is those it shelters.” He died before knowing which parts Edric obeyed and can testify to his own words and priorities, not Edric's later motives. Branoc favors evacuation, distributed stores, living scouts, and authority limited to named communities, but he is not automatically competent to direct a changed war. His answer is historical and constitutional evidence, not present-day command.

references.title: Lady Aderyn Taran
references.summary: Widow of Mael's elder brother and holder of founder authority, able to support delay, witnessed seizure, and a replacement defense without claiming the throne or settling cauldron ownership.
references.content:
## Near the throne, not seated

Lady Aderyn Taran is the widow of Mael's elder brother. She holds household keys, old servants, the founder's seal, and the right to speak before her son's inheritance is sworn around him, but she is near the throne rather than seated on it. She repeats no sentence she has not chosen to own and measures every proposal against the morning after.

## The morning after

Aderyn wants Branoc's testimony heard without leaving the vale leaderless. She supplied Gwyne with information, withheld the founder's seal until the ring could be tested, and prepared a defense covenant joining roads, grain, scouts, watch duty, and expiring authority. She asks who will witness Branoc, who chooses the first question, where the cauldron will rest afterward, and what living command remains if the old Compact fails.

## What the founder's seal can open

Aderyn's seal can authenticate founder provisions, open old mechanisms, support the Night of Hearing, require delay over authenticated testimony, and lend public standing to a witnessed seizure or replacement covenant. It does not reveal Branoc's command, make Gwyne's accusation true, bind Vane or Hew without their assent, award the cauldron, or create unilateral royal title. Her current allegiance, willingness to release the seal, and final custody position remain matters for play.

references.title: Brother Caddoc
references.summary: Exacting hereditary keeper of the Full Asking who can authenticate Branoc's ring, conduct the rite, and serve as chapel witness while bearing responsibility for Mael's damaging trials.
references.content:
## Keeper without the title

Brother Caddoc is the cauldron's hereditary keeper without the title Mael recognizes. He is exact about ritual verbs: the dead are *invited*, never raised, and *depart*, never dismissed. He joined the first borrowed-counsel trials to save the northern bridges and continued after seeing the cost because he feared an untrained operator would destroy the cauldron. That defense explains his complicity and does not absolve it.

## Nine silences and one witness

Caddoc keeps the complete Full Asking, the nine faculties, the custody clause, the Night of Hearing, the carrying calendar, and the chapel's royal wax casts. He can provisionally authenticate Branoc's ring, conduct the rite, serve as chapel witness, open the Barrow Stair through his keeper phrase, and explain the last reversible interval before a silence is committed. His authority concerns ritual integrity, testimony, and keeping; it is not founder authority, military surety, ownership, or a power to compel the dead.

## The question before the key

Caddoc asks where an anchor came from, what exact question will be asked, who will witness, and who will keep the cauldron afterward. Threats may force access but cannot produce competent help. A recovered reason may let one borrowed answer qualify or retract its command, but it does not restore a complete person or replenish a spent silence. Caddoc's present obedience, location, keys, and willingness to accompany the vessel remain matters for play.

references.title: Edric Taran
references.summary: House Taran's western-gate commander, whose later recital became the Gate Compact's hereditary emergency doctrine even though no surviving record carries Branoc's own hand or seal.
references.content:
## The recital that became law

After the western-gate crisis, Edric Taran testified that Branoc ordered him to close the gate, abandon the outer ward, and preserve Dunwarren at any cost. The earliest surviving Compact identifies those words as Edric's sworn account after Branoc and the outer-ward witnesses were dead, displaced, or voiceless. Later renewals silently recast the recital as direct royal command and built House Taran's emergency privileges upon it.

## Wicket, stair, and outer ward

Branoc actually ordered Edric to bar the great leaves against the riders, keep the wicket and river stair open until the outer ward was within, and abandon the fort if necessary to save the people. Edric closed the wicket and river stair before the outer ward was inside, held the fortress, and later preserved only the first command in his recital. Branoc died before learning which portions Edric obeyed.

## What his oath cannot settle

Edric's recital is a consequential witness statement, not Branoc's own recorded answer and not proof of Mael's present authority. Branoc can establish his command and priorities but cannot establish Edric's later motives. Judgment of Edric's conduct, land restoration, memorial correction, compensation, succession, and blame require living evidence and political action beyond the Full Asking.

references.title: Captain Rhod Vane
references.summary: Captain of Dunwarren's living guard, whose bounded orders, sacred-object recovery articles, and concern for a defensible morning can separate civil protection from Mael's disputed ritual command.
references.content:
## Orders bounded by bell and place

Captain Rhod Vane commands Dunwarren's living guard through explicit orders bounded by place, object, bell, and lawful purpose. He carries the living-guard keys and deliberately carries no key to the Cauldron Vault. When borrowed voices disagree, household posts hold position and seek his judgment rather than treating every dead answer as command.

## Preserve the water

Vane's standing articles for sacred household objects forbid arrows, fire, hooked blades, and mounted pursuit wherever cauldron water might be spilled. Guards are to hold routes, preserve the water, take bearers living, and seize wheels, ropes, doors, or the named keeper before striking the vessel. Mael can countermand those articles, but a public countermand exposes the distance between preserving the institution and recovering it at any cost.

## What he can secure

Vane can secure doors and roads, withdraw or redirect patrols, preserve witnesses, recognize a bounded replacement defense, and serve as military surety for a Night of Hearing. He does not authenticate anchors, keep the rite, supply founder authority, own the cauldron, or settle constitutional title. His present allegiance, guard posture, available keys, and willingness to oppose a particular order remain matters for play.

references.title: Mother Eluned
aliases: Mother Eluned of the Mere House
references.summary: Senior surviving Nine Hearth keeper and patron of the Green Larks, pressing a serious but incomplete communal-custody claim against both Mael and any coalition that would make another royal use precede three-hearth deliberation.
references.content:
## The Mere House keeper

Mother Eluned of the Mere House is senior among the surviving Nine Hearth keepers and acts for the remaining Trust. She hired the Green Larks to recover the cauldron intact, declare temporary Trust custody, and carry the vessel to Mere House before another ruler turns it into an instrument of immediate need.

## Three hearths before another question

Eluned insists that future use return to communal keeping. She rejects a royal Asking before three hearths can convene because the cauldron was built as a circuit among communities, not as the possession of whichever court can reach it. The exact first question, Branoc's consent, the dawn deadline, unabridged witness leaves, and genuinely shared custody can force her agents to distinguish necessary testimony from permanent royal precedent.

## What seniority cannot settle

Eluned may convene surviving hearths, recognize a receiving keeper, seat the bands at Mere House, and press the Trust's older custody claim. Only three complete keeper lines survive, two broken seals contest seniority, and the old law never anticipated a stolen anchor, coerced Muster, and renewal oath on the same night. She offers a legitimate claimant and destination, not a final judgment or uncontested ownership. Her present instructions, willingness to compromise, and recognition of any temporary keeper remain matters for play.

references.title: Tomas Wren
references.summary: Courteous Green Lark leader and transport specialist who turns threats into shared carrying problems, brings Mother Eluned’s rival commission into the heist, and demands a receiving keeper before movement becomes custody.
references.content:
## A road to Mere House

Tomas Wren leads the Green Lark recovery party sent by Mother Eluned. He enters Dunwarren at the third bell and treats every claim as a road, load, hand, boat, and destination someone must actually provide. He wants the cauldron intact at Mere House and regards Branoc's urgent first question as important evidence obtained through a dangerous royal precedent.

## Skiff, crossbeam, and bargain

Tomas can provide a second skiff, four skilled extraction hands, tow lines, a folding crossbeam, false pursuit signs, and quiet movement through the reeds. He bargains when another crew controls the route and seizes logistics when refused: capstan, winding bar, tow line, unattended anchor, or the public custody claim itself. At the final threshold he must name Eluned and the Trust or relinquish the pretense that he is moving the vessel for no patron.

## Receiver, not owner

Tomas is a receiving agent and transport leader, not owner, ritual keeper, founder authority, or the whole Trust. Possession of a boat, rope, ring, or cradle does not grant authority for a Full Asking. The exact question, dawn clause, Branoc's conditions, and divided temporary keeping may move him; his route, crew strength, equipment, current bargains, and control of any objective remain matters for play.

references.title: Marshal Hew Pale
references.summary: Marshal of the damaged field command and keeper of the war roll, seeking actionable counsel for a real northern threat while remaining capable of replacing extracted answers with a living intelligence and engineering council.
references.content:
## The war roll at his wrist

Marshal Hew Pale keeps the war roll and measures danger in seasons, road days, grain figures, uncertain bridges, and scouts returned. Red Fen killed or scattered a third of his field command. He needs a defensible morning and will not accept ritual purity as a substitute for current maps, engineers, stores, ferrymen, and officers able to issue orders.

## A living council by morning

Hew knows that a fact is not a plan. He can verify the military names selected for the Great Muster, insist on narrow actionable questions, serve as military surety for a Night of Hearing, and chair a living council of scouts, engineers, granary keepers, and valley captains. Evidence that stripped answers cannot rank competing goods can move him from the Muster toward that council.

## Military surety, not title

Hew does not authenticate Branoc, keep the cauldron, grant founder authority, or decide whether Edric's recital created lawful present title. His strategic need cannot make extracted expertise into consent or living command. His current support for Mael, access to the war roll, military deployments, and willingness to accept a replacement covenant remain matters for play.

references.title: Nessa Pike
references.summary: Mistress of Dunwarren's kitchens, whose tally authority, worker protection, household memory, and control of bells, carts, and service routes give ordinary people leverage over the heist's noble and ritual claims.
references.content:
## Every body, bowl, key, and ladle

Nessa Pike runs Dunwarren's kitchens through counts, cords, tasks, bells, stores, and the knowledge that every body, bowl, key, and ladle belongs somewhere. She will conceal competent help, expose anyone who endangers her staff, and oppose Mael's steward when workers are counted as equipment. Her authority is practical, immediate, and older than the court the kitchens feed.

## Bells, carts, and kitchen witnesses

Nessa controls the first two serving bells, can delay a count, hide one person, clear the staff yard, place the reinforced cart, and turn kitchen workers into witnesses around a moving load. Her household rules preserve reasons omitted from several borrowed answers: stores exist for people, triage protects the lives that sustain others, and no key should close every route.

## What she will not carry

Nessa can lend ordinary-household legitimacy and material support, but she will not burn, poison, abandon an injured worker, or carry a sacred burden merely to settle a noble quarrel. She has no ritual keeping, founder authority, military command, or permanent custody claim. Her present protection, bell timing, available labor, and willingness to open a route remain matters for play.

references.title: Efa Rill
references.summary: Mason and named excavation witness who removed Branoc's oath-ring before Mael closed the chamber, preserving the first viable chain from the western-gate remains to the anchor without claiming more than she observed.
references.content:
## What the fallen stone exposed

Efa Rill worked the emergency underpinning beneath Dunwarren's western gate. When the roof settled into a chamber absent from every surviving plan, she saw the crowned skeleton, the inward fall, the blade wound, and the order in which officers and workers arrived. Before Mael's men declared the remains plague dead and closed the work, she removed the worn gold oath-ring from the skeleton's hand.

## Sequence before inference

Efa speaks in sequence and stone: which course moved, what fell, where the body lay, what dust held the missing object's impression, and who reached the chamber before it was sealed. She will testify only if her name and act are preserved rather than used as an invisible source. Her account joins the ring to Branoc's chamber and exposes the searches and arrests that followed the coalition's failed neutral-hearing offer.

## What her witness can establish

Efa can establish provenance and the conduct of the excavation. She cannot authenticate the ring's private oath-name, prove Branoc's command, know Edric's motives, or decide Mael's present authority. Her injury, location, protection, willingness to enter Dunwarren, and availability as a live witness remain matters for play.

references.title: The Green Larks
references.summary: A mobile recovery crew hired by Mother Eluned to take the cauldron intact to Mere House, using distractions, transport craft, route opportunism, and custody bargaining rather than treating the vessel as ordinary loot.
references.content:
## A keeper's knot, not a buyer's purse

The Green Larks are a professional recovery crew acting for Mother Eluned and the surviving Nine Hearth Trust. They enter Dunwarren at the third bell under a court distraction and seek the cauldron intact before Mael or Gwyne's coalition turns emergency possession into precedent. Their keeper's knot and carrying token mark a custodial commission, not a buyer's purse.

## Take the road another crew neglects

The Larks exploit neglected routes, compromised workers, false objectives, tow lines, skiffs, capstans, and other crews' abandoned equipment. They lack a dedicated roof specialist but are strong at movement, disguise, and bargaining around a load. When opposed, they prefer seizing logistics or forcing a public custody declaration to breaking the vessel or beginning an indiscriminate fight.

## Movement is not keeping

The Larks can move and preserve the target, produce witnesses, and make Mere House a concrete destination. They do not embody the whole Trust, decide permanent ownership, authenticate Branoc, or become keepers by physical possession. Their members present, route, equipment, objectives controlled, and current compact with another crew remain in encounters, ledgers, and play state.

references.title: The Nine Hearth Trust
references.summary: The surviving remnant of a nine-community funerary circuit that kept the cauldron in rotation before House Taran's continuous emergency custody, preserving a serious communal claim without supplying one uncontested owner.
references.content:
## Nine hearths on one road

Nine communities once kept the cauldron in rotation along a carrying road. Their trust treated custody as a circuit of named keepers and destinations rather than a throne or permanent household possession. House Taran's fifty-three years of renewed emergency custody interrupted that practice without erasing every line, seal, or obligation.

## Three surviving keeper lines

Mere, Rowan, and Bell retain complete keeper lines. Two further claims survive through broken seals and descendant households. Mother Eluned, senior keeper at Mere House, presses the Trust's claim and commissions the Green Larks to recover the vessel before another royal use. A three-hearth council can recognize receiving custody and deliberate over future use.

## What three hearths cannot decide

Three hearths are not nine, disputed seals challenge Eluned's seniority, and the old circuit did not foresee a stolen personal anchor, a coerced Great Muster, and a dawn renewal oath together. The Trust can supply history, keepers, destination, and a rival lawful framework. It cannot alone settle permanent ownership, Branoc's first question, the current defense, or every community's consent. Which seals, keepers, and temporary terms are accepted remains a matter for play.

references.title: The Cauldron of Nine Silences
references.summary: A communal funerary vessel and nine-banded oak cradle whose accumulated silences can invite one honored dead person as a person, while movement, custody, and any spent faculty remain distinct operational problems.
references.content:
## One person through nine silences

The Cauldron of Nine Silences is a funerary vessel, not a resurrection engine or an ordinary instrument for questioning corpses. Through a true personal anchor and witnessed invitation, it can receive one honored dead person in voice, memory, judgment, and will. Its power accumulated through nine communal silences kept across generations.

## Face, Road, Measure, Hearth

Nine iron bands hold those silences in relation. Face preserves recognition; Road, ordered memory; Measure, judgment; Hearth, affection; Hand, self-command; Season, temporal understanding; Bar, refusal; Reply, reciprocal speech; and Rest, voluntary departure. They are not interchangeable charges. A committed or damaged band removes a named faculty and may require communal restoration over years or generations.

## The keeper at the threshold

The bronze vessel and living-oak cradle form one operating object. Four custody dogs govern movement without opening a ritual band. Consecrated thresholds require a living keeper, destination, and authority for future use; possession of vessel, keys, wheels, or ropes does not replace that declaration. Current band condition, dog state, load, route, testimony, custody, and restoration progress belong to `VAULT-OPERATIONS.md`, `EXTRACTION-AND-AFTERMATH.md`, encounters, and play state.

references.title: Branoc's Oath-Ring
references.summary: The newly recovered intimate anchor that can identify and invite Branoc through private name, lifetime wear, royal flaw, and chamber provenance, while proving neither his command nor its holder's authority.
references.content:
## The hand beneath the gate

Efa Rill removed the gold oath-ring from the hand of the crowned skeleton exposed beneath Dunwarren's western gate. The chamber mortar, the missing impression in the hand's dust, the ring's private oath-name, its royal wax flaw, and wear from long bodily use connect the object to Branoc more closely than public regalia or inherited legend could.

## An invitation, not an answer

The ring is the first viable personal anchor found since Branoc's death. Chapel records and royal wax casts can authenticate its marks, allowing the Full Asking to invite Branoc as a person rather than a title assembled from public memory. The anchor permits an invitation; it does not compel acceptance or predetermine an answer.

## What old gold cannot prove

The ring establishes identity and provenance. It does not prove what Branoc commanded, validate Edric's recital, transfer cauldron custody, grant royal title, or make its possessor Branoc's agent. Its current bearer, concealment, damage, seizure, and route remain matters for encounters, the heist ledger, and play state.

references.title: The Gate Compact
references.summary: The repeatedly renewed emergency covenant built on Edric Taran's recital of Branoc's western-gate command, joining House Taran's control of defense and custody to a historical claim now subject to exact testimony.
references.content:
## Edric's recital beneath every renewal

The Gate Compact rests on Edric Taran's sworn recital that Branoc ordered the western gate closed and Dunwarren preserved. No surviving copy carries Branoc's own hand or seal. Later renewals treated Edric's report as direct royal command and let House Taran claim roads, grain, levies, noble wards, and cauldron custody whenever danger was declared.

## Dawn oath and noon hearing

The seven valleys renew the Compact at dawn. Each household brings a memorial roll for the customary recitation of service; Mael has joined those rolls into the Great Muster's war register and means to present its answer before the oath. One authenticated witness leaf and two living witnesses can invoke the Compact's contradiction procedure and stay renewal until noon, creating a hearing rather than an automatic verdict.

## What the Compact cannot inherit

The Compact can organize real defense and preserve existing offices while its terms remain accepted. It cannot prove the recital on which it rests, make the Great Muster consensual counsel, settle permanent cauldron ownership, or turn Branoc's eventual testimony into present-day command. Which households swear, delay, refuse, or accept a replacement covenant remains a matter for play.

references.title: The Full Asking
references.summary: The complete witnessed invitation by which one honored dead person may return in voice, memory, judgment, and will, answer or refuse freely, and leave an exact record without acquiring rule over the living present.
references.content:
## Name, question, witness, keeper

A Full Asking invites one honored dead person through a true personal anchor. It requires the whole name, an honest first question, willing witnesses, the dead person's consent, nine intact silences, and named living custody afterward. The dead returns in voice, memory, judgment, and will rather than as a reconstructed body or a store of literal facts.

## Freedom in the water

The invited person may answer, refuse, challenge the question, accuse, forgive, qualify, admit uncertainty, ask questions in return, impose conditions, or depart. The promised first question for Branoc remains: *What command did you give Edric Taran at the western gate?* Three black-water leaves can preserve the whole exchange, including objections, uncertainty, and replies from the living.

## Testimony, not command

A complete answer supplies testimony and governing priorities, not self-executing law. Branoc can establish his own words and ask what followed; he cannot inspect the present road from memory or decide every later motive, succession, restoration, defense, or custody question. The Night of Hearing may secure one night for an Asking through chapel witness, founder authority, and military surety, but permanent ownership and present command remain unresolved.

references.title: The Great Muster
references.summary: Mael's fifth-bell mass extraction, using household memorial rolls, copper combs, and the cauldron's accumulated silences to obtain accurate military answers after severing the reasons and attachments that once governed them.
references.content:
## Hundreds of names beneath one question

The Great Muster converts the households' memorial rolls into a chained war register and addresses narrow military questions to many honored dead. Copper name combs, band keys, question boards, and the underkeep command network extract useful answers without inviting those dead as whole persons. Mael intends to present the result as inherited service before the dawn renewal.

## Answers without reasons

The answers remain factually competent within their domains, but the rite strips away love, fear, loyalty, promise, and purpose. The result cannot rank grain against people, walls against households, speed against the wounded, or victory against those made to bear it. Each committed band spends a named communal silence and diminishes future Full Askings for generations. Earlier trial needles created the twelve borrowed voices without committing a whole band.

## What the Muster cannot make lawful

The Muster may produce actionable military information. It does not create consent, restore context, authenticate Branoc, prove Edric's recital, renew the Gate Compact by itself, or grant Mael permanent custody. Which names, questions, combs, bands, answers, and living posts are active remains in the heist, underkeep, and vault operating sheets and in play state.

encounters.title: The Crooked Magpie
encounters.summary: A ruined tide-road tavern offers Branoc's ring, one exact question, three approaches, and a custody dispute already waiting at the exit.
encounters.opening_view: The rain reaches the ring before Gwyne Marr does. One drop strikes the lead box between three cups, an unanswered letter, and Sib Crowle’s open tide book. Across the mere, fresh scaffolding braces Dunwarren’s western gate while feast lamps climb the hill toward dawn. Gwyne watches both preparations, then asks which danger the crew means to prevent.
encounters.content:
## Situation

The Crooked Magpie did not close all at once. First Lord Mael diverted the tide road. Then the carriers stopped, the floor warped toward the mere, and Sib Crowle began serving only people who preferred a ruined house to a witnessed meeting. Rain works at the shutters. Across the flats, Dunwarren shines with midsummer lamps while seven valleys send masks, musicians, wine, and sworn representatives uphill to renew the Gate Compact at dawn.

Five weeks ago, the levy screen broke at Red Fen and Dunwarren lost a third of its field command. Mael ordered the western gate underpinned before the northern host could test it again. Three weeks ago, that work settled through a chamber absent from every surviving plan. The masons found a crowned skeleton beneath the inward-fallen roof, a blade wound under its ribs. Mael’s officers called the bones plague dead and closed the work before noon. **Efa Rill** had already taken one object from the skeleton’s hand: a gold oath-ring, worn thin at the inner edge.

The ring rests on the Magpie’s table in a lead box. Its private oath-name, old wax flaw, bodily wear, and gate mortar establish one thing: the cauldron can invite Branoc as a person. They say nothing about what he commanded. Gwyne makes that boundary the price of touching it.

## The commission

Gwyne speaks for a narrow, mutually suspicious coalition: descendants of households left outside the western gate, two jurists who distrust the Compact's recital, an abbot who once kept the cauldron's rites, and Lady Aderyn Taran, whose support remains deniable even within the coalition. Payment is old silver, clean passage from the vale, and patrons who will deny the meeting.

The commission has two named successes. **Bring out the cauldron intact, with its oak cradle and nine iron bands, before the fifth bell.** If removal fails, conduct Branoc's Full Asking inside Dunwarren before the Great Muster. Sabotage may save tonight and still leave Branoc unheard, the instrument damaged, and Mael in possession.

The coalition's agreed first question is written on a single strip of vellum:

> What command did you give Edric Taran at the western gate?

The question assumes neither an open gate nor Edric's guilt nor Branoc's murder. Gwyne has accused House Taran for twenty years. She will not purchase vindication by leading the first answer that can test her charge.

## Why tonight

Put three deadlines on the planning table.

1. **The anchor is new.** Branoc has never been summoned. His body and intimate regalia were believed destroyed until the gate chamber opened.
2. **The law is about to harden.** At dawn, the assembled nobles renew the Gate Compact by swearing to preserve the vale “as Branoc commanded at the western gate.” If they hear contrary testimony first, many cannot swear. If they swear first, undoing the new obligations may require rebellion rather than refusal.
3. **The cauldron is about to be spent.** Mael will use the fifth bell to begin a Great Muster. Instead of inviting one dead person through a true anchor, his rite burns the nine silences accumulated in the cauldron's bands and tears military counsel from hundreds of honored dead named on the war roll. Brother Caddoc believes nothing sufficient for a Full Asking will remain afterward.

The coalition offered chapel authentication under Caddoc, Aderyn's founder authority, and an opposed household jurist. Mael demanded sole emergency custody, declared the cauldron a military instrument, moved it into the drowned court, imprisoned Efa's foreman, and searched the masons' houses. Gwyne withdrew the ring from an inquiry Mael alone could close. The heist begins where that bounded lawful offer ended.

## What the crew knows

- Dunwarren's public court, kitchens, roofs, chapel, and underkeep were built in different centuries and do not share one security system.
- The feast creates three plausible approaches: enter among masked guests, enter with the kitchen train, or cross the roofs from the old rook tower.
- The cauldron is black bronze, broad enough to bathe a body, and fixed to an oak carrying cradle by nine iron bands. The bands store the accumulated silences; damaging them may make the Full Asking partial or impossible.
- The proper rite returns one honored dead person in voice, memory, judgment, and will. It does not compel an answer.
- Mael has tested his corrupted method on twelve honored dead with hair-fine needles through still-closed bands. Fragments of their counsel now speak in the House of Borrowed Voices below the chapel; the trials strained the instrument without yet spending a whole silence.
- The Reed Weir opens to the tidal mere at low water. Gwyne has arranged a flat-bottomed boat, but nobody yet knows how to open the inner grate.
- Mael knows a small royal object was removed from the gate chamber because its impression remained in the dead hand's mortar dust. He does not know who holds it, and he may not know it is Branoc's oath-ring.
- Each household delegation has brought a memorial roll for the renewal feast. Mael's clerks are chaining those rolls into the Great Muster's war register, which is why hundreds of named dead and the nobles asked to receive their counsel are present on the same night.

## Cast

- **Gwyne Marr** keeps the question strip beside the lead box. She marks every claim as *establishes*, *suggests*, or *does not prove*, and stops the table whenever anyone treats the ring, Edric's recital, or her own ancestry as Branoc's answer.
- **Efa Rill** places her bandaged wrist beside the ring and reconstructs the collapse with cups and the lead box. She will enter Dunwarren only if the crew puts her name beside the act instead of using her as an invisible source.
- **Tomas Wren**, rain-dark coat still wet, takes an unoffered chair and turns every threat into a transport problem. The Green Larks enter at the third bell whether the crew accepts cooperation or merely leaves them a road.
- **Sib Crowle**, the Magpie’s former keeper, measures courage in tides, invoices, and how far a handcart must be pushed under fire. She will not enter Dunwarren. She will provide tide tables, staff gossip, storage, and a false cooper’s mark, then tell the crew which favor has become a debt.

## The planning table

Put four lists before the players: **approach**, **cover**, **target handling**, and **testimony**. Each commitment buys an advantage and names a risk; leave the rest open for adaptation.

### Approaches

**Masked guests.** Gwyne can provide one genuine invitation and enough household knowledge to improvise the rest. The seal passes a quick inspection, but Dunwarren verifies important guests through a living witness. The crew must recruit, deceive, replace, or avoid that witness.

**Kitchen train.** Sib can place the crew on a late ale or charcoal cart. The kitchens are hot, crowded, and permeable. They also count every worker at the second bell and close the east passage whenever the serving bells are wrong.

**Rook tower.** The ruined tower stands outside the inner wall and is reachable from the tide road. A chain walk once connected it to the keep roof. The chains remain, but their boards were removed after a smuggler's hanging.

Reward coordination across doors. The crew need not enter together.

### Covers and assets

Gwyne and Sib can assemble three strong assets before the first bell. Each additional asset costs time, creates a witness, or advances the rival crew.

- A genuine invitation naming a dead knight whose face is not widely known.
- Two servant tabards and a tally of the current kitchen shifts.
- A coil of tarred rope, roof hooks, and a narrow plank.
- A cooper's handcart reinforced to carry an unusually heavy cask.
- An old copy of the Full Asking rubric, missing the custodial clause and final witness response.
- A shallow impression of the founder's seal, too blurred for close ceremonial use.
- A sleeping draught strong enough for one cup, not a whole table.
- A tide key that fits the outer Reed Weir lock but not the inner grate.
- Efa Rill as a living witness to the gate chamber, at the cost of placing her inside Mael's reach.

### Target and testimony questions

- How many of the nine silences remain whole after Mael's experiments?
- Can the oak cradle be dismantled or substituted without dispersing the stored power?
- What causes the twelve borrowed voices to warn the fort when the cauldron moves?
- Can Brother Caddoc perform a Full Asking away from Dunwarren?
- What makes Branoc's oath-ring an accepted anchor rather than merely old gold?
- Who must witness Branoc for the testimony to matter before the Gate Compact is sworn?
- Does the coalition intend to publish Branoc's whole answer even if it condemns its own cause?

## The bell clock

Before the first bell, the crew can gather assets, recruit one inside contact, or test one approach. At the first bell the White Hart gates open and the kitchen count begins. At the second, Mael announces the Great Muster and presents the Gate Compact for dawn renewal. At the third, the Green Larks enter behind a planned court distraction. At the fourth, Mael descends with the war roll and begins opening the nine band-locks. The low-tide extraction window follows. At the fifth bell, the Great Muster begins unless prevented. Dawn brings the renewal oath.

End planning when the crew commits to at least one route into Dunwarren and names the bearer of the oath-ring. A return before the first bell is free; after the feast begins, each return costs a pressure step and risks Sib, Efa, or Gwyne's coalition.

## The nine hearth marks

Sib's tide book predates the Magpie. Its inside board bears nine hearths joined by a carrying road, the mark once burned onto carts that moved the cauldron from settlement to settlement. Gwyne recognizes the sign. Before House Taran claimed continuous emergency custody, nine communities kept the vessel in rotation. Three still maintain complete keeper lines; two others survive through disputed seals and descendant households. The old trust is therefore neither dead nor able to speak with one uncontested voice.

After Branoc speaks, Gwyne proposes Mere House under Caddoc, one outer-ward keeper, and one representative acceptable to Aderyn. She copied that proposal to Mother Eluned because no threshold accepts *away* as a destination. Eluned refused a royal Asking before a three-hearth council and sent Tomas Wren to recover the vessel first. The Green Larks carry a keeper's knot, not a buyer's purse, and Gwyne's notice gave their rival claim a road into the heist.

encounters.title: The White Hart Court
encounters.summary: Mael turns hospitality, memorial rolls, and Red Fen's dead into a public argument for inherited emergency power.
encounters.opening_view: “Wax admits the paper,” calls the first herald. “A witness admits the person.” Masked households pass beneath the white antlers while clerks bind their memorial rolls into one iron register. Musicians play over the chain’s scrape. Captain Vane’s guards carry shields and rope knives, but no bows face the sacred hill. At the fire, Mael rehearses Branoc’s command before Branoc has spoken.
encounters.content:
## Situation

The White Hart Court is gate, feast yard, and throne room with the roof taken off. Red rushes hide the mud. Musicians play above the portcullis. The central fire is large enough to feed the court and bright enough to lend every mask the same honest expression. Mael has made abundance part of his constitutional argument: Dunwarren feeds the vale; therefore Dunwarren must command it.

Every courtesy leans toward tomorrow’s oath. The oldest recital says Branoc ordered Edric Taran to close the western gate, abandon the outer ward, and preserve the stronghold at any cost. House Taran has drawn roads, grain, levies, and noble wards from that sentence whenever danger is declared. Red Fen makes the danger real: a third of Hew's field command is dead or scattered, and the northern road depends on scouts and two uncertain bridges. Mael means the old emergency to explain the new obedience.

The court is open by categories, not by trust. Wax admits a document; a living witness admits a person. Servants pass by tally, performers by search, lesser guests under a greater household. Difficult arrivals are not dragged away. They are seated near the gate, given wine, and placed where Captain Rhod Vane can count every door they look at.

## Cast

- **Lord Mael Taran** stands between the central fire and the chained memorial rolls, correcting wagon counts while the herald speaks. Challenge the Muster and he records the objection, then asks who commands the wagons, keeps the western gate, holds the ring, and answers for the next dead patrol.
- **Captain Rhod Vane** keeps the living-guard keys at the gate table and gives orders by door, object, and bell. Show him counsel stripped of its conditions, and he asks which order remains lawful tonight.
- **Lady Aderyn Taran** wears no mask. She names every servant who approaches, measures proposals against morning, and leaves for the founder's seal after Mael's declaration unless the crew forces an earlier choice.
- **Marshal Hew Pale** keeps the war roll chained to his wrist. He answers claims with road days, grain figures, uncertain bridges, and scouts returned; ask whether the dead have advised him, and he looks first at the living shortages.
- **Nia Bell**, junior herald, knows invitations are being reused and altered. Procedure is the only protection her office gives her, and she has seen three masons' names added to the quiet arrest list.

## Ways through

### Pass as invited guests

A genuine invitation and plausible name clear the wax. A living witness clears the person. Recruit Aderyn, press a minor noble who owes Gwyne, replace Nia, join a noisy household, or make the heralds admit arrivals faster than they can verify them.

A failed witness seats the crew at a gate table under observation. The feast, kitchens, musicians' stair, petition bench, and holding rooms remain reachable, but Captain Vane watches every later deception.

### Enter as staff or suppliers

Kitchen carts circle behind the musicians' gallery. Their loads are opened but not individually searched. Workers are counted by colored tally cords. A correct cord gets a person into the court; a missing person on the kitchen roll creates an investigation at the second bell.

### Climb from the outer wall

The heralds never look up during an arrival. The musicians' gallery joins the Rookwalk above the portcullis. Reaching it requires the old chain bridge, a climb from the rain spouts, or access through the performers' stair.

## The second-bell declaration

At the second bell Mael raises no skull and promises no miracle. Each household has brought a memorial roll for the renewal's customary recitation of service. His clerks fasten those separate rolls into one chained war register: hundreds of honored captains, scouts, engineers, ferrymen, and physicians, presented by the same households that will receive the answer. Mael announces that at the fifth bell the cauldron will gather their counsel into one response to the question, “How shall the vale survive the northern host?” At dawn, after that response is read, the nobles will renew the Gate Compact.

Mael names every living shortage correctly and gives the number of widows after Red Fen. He calls the dead's cost a final service implied by honor. He never names the right to refuse, and he says nothing of the reasons his twelve trials left behind.

Interrupt, expose evidence, demand the war roll, or make Mael define the rite before the households. He answers narrowly without lying: the dead “are not compelled to speak falsely.” He will not say they are free to remain silent.

## Opportunities

- The compact copies quote Branoc only through Edric Taran's later testimony. No surviving line bears Branoc's hand or seal.
- Three excavation laborers are held in rooms off the gatehouse. Their presence can confirm that the western chamber was not a plague crypt, though none saw Efa take the ring.
- Captain Vane carries the living-guard keys. He never carries keys to the Cauldron Vault; he considers that separation essential.
- Marshal Hew leaves the war roll with a clerk during the first dance after Mael's speech. Altering it can spoil tonight's Muster but cannot permanently stop Mael from reconstructing the names.
- Lady Aderyn leaves for her solar after the speech and returns before the fourth bell. She can become ally, adversary, witness, or lawful claimant.
- The Green Larks use the feast as camouflage. Tomas Wren has arranged for a masked dancer to collapse at the third bell, pulling the court physician and two guards away.

## Pressure responses

The court answers suspicion socially before it answers violently.

**Noted.** A herald remembers the crew's faces, cover, carried box, or claimed household.

**Questioned.** Nia or Vane asks for a second witness, inspects an object, or separates one crew member from the others.

**Contained.** The crew is seated, escorted, or given a courteous guard. Movement remains possible through favors, confusion, a new identity, or a public petition.

**Exposed.** The gates close and the living guard searches for a specific description. The feast continues because Mael refuses to let thieves dictate the night's meaning.

## What changes here

Aderyn can witness an identity and later release the founder's seal. Evidence of counsel stripped from purpose can detach Vane's living guard from Mael's ritual command. Displaying the oath-ring forces Mael to claim custody or emergency privilege in public. Proving the Compact rests on Edric's testimony gives hesitant nobles grounds to delay the oath for a Full Asking.

## Recovery articles

Captain Vane's standing articles for sacred household objects hang behind the gate sergeant's chair. They forbid arrows, fire, hooked blades, or mounted pursuit wherever cauldron water might be spilled. Bearers are to be taken alive when possible; guards seize wheels, ropes, doors, and the named keeper rather than striking the vessel. Mael can countermand the articles, but doing so before witnesses exposes that he values immediate control above the institution he claims to protect.

The renewal oath carries its own restraint. One authenticated black-water leaf, supported by two named witnesses, stays the oath until noon and summons opposed witnesses when it contradicts the Compact's recital. It decides no succession, guilt, or custody; it stops the households from swearing a known abridgment in Branoc's name.

encounters.title: The Smoke Kitchens
encounters.summary: Soot, tallies, serving bells, and overworked staff govern the keep more precisely than its nobles suspect.
encounters.opening_view: Three hundred plates. Nine copper combs warming by the furnace. Two colors of pipe case where only one should be. Nessa Pike catches the wrong knot on a charcoal carrier’s tabard and closes the tally board with her burned hand. An ash cart waits beside the third-bell door. The kitchens do not stop for strangers; they may, however, put them to work.
encounters.content:
## Situation

Dunwarren’s kitchens are older than the court they feed. Hearths press against a pre-conquest wall; ovens, cisterns, sculleries, stores, and sleeping shelves fill the remaining space. Too many bodies can hide a stranger. Nessa's count can expose one, because every body, bowl, key, and ladle belongs somewhere.

Three bells govern the work. The first sends bread and meat upward. The second returns platters and releases half the scullions. The third clears the east passage for ash carts before the final service. For seven minutes, no living guard stands between that passage and the obsolete road below the chapel. The opening is not secret. It survives because the people who know it are usually too busy carrying other people’s feast.

## Cast

- **Nessa Pike**, mistress of kitchens, is small, burned along one forearm, and impossible to hurry. She despises Lord Mael's steward for counting workers who sleep in her kitchens as if they were spoons. She will conceal competent help and expose anyone who endangers her staff.
- **Bran Tallow**, cellarer, sells access in small increments: a cord, a key impression, a quiet stair, a missing cask. He is already taking money from the Green Larks and will serve both crews until forced to choose.
- **Melly Reed**, ash girl, knows the undercroft by smell and echo. Her family keeps the memorial song of Captain Alwen Reed. Since Mael tested the borrowed-counsel rite on Alwen, the verse naming the ferrymen he saved has vanished from every written copy, and Melly dreams of a man who remembers the river but not the people in it.
- **Brother Caddoc**, keeper of the Last Word, comes for heated spring water before every bell. He uses it to warm the copper throats in the House of Borrowed Voices. He carries the chapel key openly because nobody in the kitchens wants his work.

## Operating the room

Make every intrusion take a job. Trenchers move toward court. Spits keep a character near Nessa. Casks reach the cellar ramp. Ash opens the east passage and leaves soot for later witnesses.

### The tally

Workers wear braided cords: red for hearths, gray for stores, yellow for service, and black for ash. Nessa's slate records names only for permanent staff; temporary workers are counted by cord and task. A forged cord survives a glance. A crew member who does no plausible work is challenged by another worker before a guard notices.

### The serving bells

The bells are rung from a rope beside the pastry hearth. Nessa controls the first two. Bran Tallow is supposed to ring the third when the steward's board returns. Ringing early clears the east passage but disrupts the feast, brings the steward down, and gives the Green Larks their planned entry signal. Delaying it leaves the route guarded but strands two ash carts in the kitchen, creating concealment and resentment.

### The ash passage

Beyond the east passage, a brick chute drops to an old cart way beneath the chapel. It is steep, greasy, and too narrow for the cauldron's cradle. It is an excellent route for people, tools, the oath-ring, or a dismantled hoist. At the bottom, one branch reaches the Barrow Stair and another drains toward the Reed Weir through a locked iron grate.

## Discoveries and leverage

- A kitchen order requests twelve covered bowls of heated spring water for the House of Borrowed Voices. Each bowl is labeled with a dead captain's name and a question Mael's clerks have forbidden the servants to read.
- Bran's payment token from Tomas Wren proves the Green Larks intend to use the third bell.
- Melly can identify three families whose memorial texts changed after Mael's trials. Their losses are not forgotten facts in living minds; the dead themselves have ceased to carry the reasons behind what they knew, and the surviving records are beginning to follow them.
- The cooper's ramp and flour rollers can move the oak cradle once it reaches this level. Doing so wrecks the last service and makes secrecy impossible.
- The inner Reed Weir grate uses a kitchen spit as its removable winding bar. Nessa keeps it above the cold hearth because the steward repeatedly loses purpose-made tools.
- Scraps from the war roll arrive as kindling. They list captains, engineers, scouts, and healers, confirming that the Great Muster seeks many narrow answers rather than one summoned council.

## Failure and escalation

A mistake brings labor before steel. Nessa demands an explanation and a useful hand; Bran prices the information; the steward detains someone for Vane. Violence, fire, poison, or a clear attack on Mael brings armed guards at once.

Earn Nessa's protection and she can hide one person, delay a count, choose a bell, or place the reinforced cart. She will not carry a sacred burden to settle a noble quarrel. Show her what the Muster consumes, or what Branoc's answer changes for people who still eat tomorrow.

## The east service rise

The ash passage broadens below the ovens into an old service rise worked by a capstan in the cooper's room. Its platform was built for winter barrels and accepts the cauldron's oak runners with two fingers to spare. Four steady hands on the capstan replace most of a carrying team, but the platform stops at kitchen level. From there the target must pass as a broad cooper's load through the staff yard and east postern.

A chalk table beside the capstan gives the cauldron and cradle six burden marks before bearers, evidence, or tools. The figures match the Rookwalk windlass and Reed Weir punt. Nessa can clear the yard with a false grease fire or surround the load with household witnesses. She will stop the lift before she abandons an injured worker.

encounters.title: The Rookwalk
encounters.summary: Broken chains and message rooks offer speed, surveillance, and a spectacular extraction route that cannot remain secret.
encounters.opening_view: The brass-ringed rook screams at the lantern, not at you. Rain runs along two load chains above the broken bridge, and each gust knocks the old lifting hook inside its tower. Court, chapel, kitchens, and western gate lie open to this height. One shutter governs the birds. The windlass beside it was built for cargo no rook could carry.
encounters.content:
## Situation

The Rookwalk once carried messages and light loads from the outer rook tower to the gallery above the gate. Smugglers cost it its boards; the two load chains remain, black with rain and fixed deep in both towers. Beyond the gallery, one broken line of slate joins the chapel cote, Aderyn’s balcony, six kitchen chimneys, and the disused siege lift above the underkeep.

No one owns the whole view. Gate guards leave the roof to the rook keeper; musicians leave it to the watch; the watch trusts anyone moving with household confidence. Rain, smoke, bells, and feast lanterns alternate blindness with moments when one body stands visible to half the fort.

## Roof elements

**The chain crossing.** A plank, crawl sling, or careful traverse crosses the gap. A fall sends someone onto the sloped gatehouse roof with noise, injury, and witnesses.

**The ringed rooks.** Dunwarren's birds carry short messages between watch posts. They cry at unfamiliar lantern colors, not unfamiliar faces. Food, darkness, a correct lantern shutter, or releasing all the birds can defeat the warning. Killing them brings the rook keeper and creates a very specific crime scene.

**The musicians' gallery.** The gallery is crowded during the first two bells and nearly empty during Mael's speech. Its back stair reaches the White Hart Court and the passage above the kitchens.

**The rain chain.** A broad copper chain drains the chapel roof into a cistern beside the Barrow Stair. It can serve as a descent line. Removing or diverting it floods the chapel aisle and exposes the older stone hatch beneath the font.

**The lifting tower.** An oak windlass once raised funeral stones from the underkeep. The cable has been cut, but the drum, brake, and roof aperture remain. Its beam carries the same nine-band maker's mark as the cauldron cradle. Re-rigged, it can lift the cradle to the roof. The first inch of movement sends breath through twelve copper speaking tubes below, waking every borrowed voice and giving the fort twelve different predictions of the theft.

## Cast

- **Ivo Rook**, keeper of the message birds, is proud of his animals and indifferent to court politics. He can be bribed with coin, enlisted through concern for the birds, or impersonated poorly because few people know his face.
- **Sella Penn**, harpist and covert correspondent for Lady Aderyn, uses the gallery to exchange messages through the rooks. She can provide a solar route and knows Aderyn expects Gwyne to act tonight.
- **Kerr and Lowen**, two young watchmen, share the chapel roof circuit. They are more worried about being blamed for wet bowstrings than about legendary thieves.

## Heist uses

Choose what the Rookwalk is buying: entry, lateral movement, surveillance, extraction, or escape. Using it for one purpose changes the others.

- Using it quietly preserves surprise but limits the crew to what they can carry by hand.
- Rebuilding the windlass creates a strong extraction route and a conspicuous fixed position.
- Releasing the rooks creates confusion across every watch post and destroys the crew's ability to intercept messages.
- Cutting the rain chain opens the chapel hatch but floods evidence and alerts Brother Caddoc.
- Crossing toward the solar gives access to Lady Aderyn's letters and seal, but places the crew above her private guard.
- Lowering a cord through the bell cote provides a route for the oath-ring or ritual papers even when the cradle must leave elsewhere.

## The rival crew

The Green Larks reach the musicians' gallery after their dancer falls at the third bell. They have no roof specialist. Control the route and Tomas bargains; damage it and he turns to the kitchens; leave gear and the Larks use it under whatever blame follows. He wants the cauldron intact for Mother Eluned and regards Branoc's question as urgent evidence obtained through a dangerous royal precedent.

## The old siege lift

The lifting tower's north windlass still aligns with the vault's north route channel. A counterweight equal to six burden marks raises the complete cradle to the roof; less requires a hauling team, and more sends the load upward hard enough to damage the stop beam. The outer siege crane can then lower it beyond the inner wall onto the tide road.

When the weir grounds, this is the fastest alternative and the least private. Rooks scatter, the roof bell sounds, and White Hart Court watches the cauldron cross the skyline. encounters.title: The Chapel of the Last Word
encounters.summary: Caddoc's chapel can authenticate Branoc, expose the wounded rite, and open the underkeep—if the crew can answer for custody.
encounters.opening_view: “Last,” says the darkness beneath the font. Brother Caddoc sets down the copper throat he has been warming and covers the chapel key with his palm. Nine black candles remain unlit. Twelve names on the memorial wall still keep their golden deeds, though ferrymen, children, rivals, and promises have been scraped away. Below, the hidden voice waits for another word.
encounters.content:
## Situation

The Chapel of the Last Word stands where household Dunwarren ends and the older underkeep begins. Nine communities built it when no lord kept the cauldron beyond one winter. Benches crowd a low room around an unraised altar. A whisper at the water reaches every witness; no keeper occupies the space between a living question and the dead.

Each black candle marks a completed communal silence: one long watch in which the hearths asked nothing of the dead and spoke every remembered name before dawn. Those silences gathered in the nine iron bands below. Together they can restore one person’s faculties without spending them. Mael’s Great Muster would separate the bands and turn that patient relation into fuel.

The injury is already legible. Twelve memorials retain their deeds and lose their reasons. Captain Alwen Reed still held the crossing for three hours, but the wall no longer names her sister’s children in the last boat. Queen Mairwen still opened the granary, but the winter children have vanished from the sentence. Caddoc has copied the stones, locked the copies away, and watched the same absences appear in ink.

## Caddoc at the candles

**Brother Caddoc** has copied the disappearing names onto fresh sheets and set them beneath the black candles. Mael calls him a household chaplain—an instrument needs maintenance, not conscience—but Caddoc corrects every ritual verb: *invite*, never *raise*; *depart*, never *dismiss*. He helped with the first trials to save the northern bridges and continued after seeing the cost because an untrained operator might ruin the cauldron at once. He names that defense and does not ask absolution for it.

Mael's hair-fine **trial needles** entered inspection holes beneath the closed Hearth, Hand, and Reply clasps. Each carried one memorial name and one narrow question, drawing a useful thread into a copper mask before the nine silences could gather around a person. Three bands are strained and twelve dead diminished; no whole silence was spent. The Great Muster opens whole bands, combs hundreds of names through water, and consumes complete faculties.

Caddoc knows Branoc has never been summoned. He also knows the newly found ring would change what is possible. He has not seen it. If shown the oath-name, the interior flaw, and the black mortar, he can authenticate it provisionally against the chapel's royal wax casts. He will then face a choice he has postponed: obey Mael's emergency warrant, or preserve the rite he was sworn to keep.

Caddoc begins cautious rather than hostile. He asks where the ring came from, who will witness Branoc, what exact question will be asked, and who will keep the cauldron afterward. Threats can force access but not competent ritual help. Evidence that Gwyne intends to accept an unwelcome answer earns more from him than outrage on behalf of the dead.

## The Full Asking

The complete rubric is distributed across the room because no single keeper was meant to control it.

1. **Anchor.** A personal object must have been carried, worn, made, or freely given by the dead person and must still bear their identity. Public regalia and copied seals are insufficient by themselves.
2. **Name.** The dead person's whole living name and one name by which they accepted honor are spoken over the water. Branoc's private oath-name is engraved inside the recovered ring.
3. **Question.** The first question is stated before the invitation. It must identify what the living genuinely seek to know. Clever ambiguity weakens the rite rather than trapping the dead.
4. **Silence.** The witnesses keep silence while the nine bands answer in sequence. Each witness must be free to leave; coerced silence produces only an echo.
5. **Consent.** The dead arrives as a person, not a record. They may answer, refuse, challenge the premise, or demand that another question be asked first.
6. **Custody.** When the Asking ends, a living keeper names where the cauldron will rest and under what authority it may next be used.

A Full Asking gives no corpse back. Water holds a presence as complete as memory permits: voice at the surface, face in depth, gestures without visible hands. The dead remembers through death, understands ordinary speech, and recognizes known people and objects. The rite ends when the dead withdraws or the ninth candle fails.

All nine silences make that fullness possible. A damaged band leaves literal, brief fragments stripped of judgment—the condition Mael exploits. Breaking the instrument stops the Muster by spending the very capacity the crew came to preserve.

## Mael's corrupted rite

The Great Muster substitutes a **war roll** for a true anchor and one broad military question for an invitation to a person. Copper combs scrape names from the roll into the water while the bands are opened separately. Each opened band forces a narrow answer from many dead at once. The answers can be accurate and still be ruinous because the dead lose the attachment that gave each answer proportion.

Caddoc's test records show the pattern:

- A ferryman remembers exactly where the channel is shallow but no longer remembers that refugees were aboard his boat.
- A queen remembers the granary inventory but not the children for whom she broke the seal.
- A captain remembers which gate can be held longest but not whom the gate was meant to save.

The stripped reasons also begin disappearing from memorial text, family dreams, and later rites. The dead are not annihilated, but they are diminished into usable expertise. Caddoc believes a complete Great Muster will damage hundreds and consume every silence sufficient for Branoc's Full Asking.

## Principal elements

**The Nine-Silence Register.** A narrow book records when each communal watch was completed, which households participated, and how strongly each iron band presently answers. All nine remain intact, though three show strain from Mael's trials.

**The petition of inquiry.** Gwyne, two jurists, and Abbot Teilo offered to present any authentic Branoc anchor in the chapel under Caddoc, Lady Aderyn's founder authority, and an opposed household witness. Mael's written refusal rejects that three-witness inspection, demands that the anchor enter his sole emergency keeping, and postpones any hearing until after the Gate Compact is renewed.

**The royal wax casts.** Six old impressions preserve the flaw and inner lettering of Branoc's oath-ring. They can authenticate Gwyne's ring without relying on her testimony alone.

**The black font.** The font conceals the upper latch of the Barrow Stair. It opens with the founder's seal, Caddoc's keeper phrase, or enough water to float the internal catch.

**The witness rail.** A copper tube runs from the vault threshold to the chapel rail. In proper use, witnesses hear the dead through it. Mael has reversed the tube so the House of Borrowed Voices can relay alarms upward.

**The preparation chest.** It contains nine band keys, witness veils, the copper name combs used in the corrupted rite, and blank custody rings. Removing the combs can delay the Great Muster. Removing or changing the keys can force Mael to open bands destructively.

## Ways to use the chapel

- Recruit Caddoc to perform Branoc's Full Asking elsewhere.
- Authenticate the oath-ring before risking public exposure.
- Take the complete ritual text and custody clause.
- Open the Barrow Stair quietly through the font.
- Reverse, block, or listen through the witness tube.
- Steal the band keys or copper combs to delay the Great Muster.
- Carry the petition, test records, or changing memorial copies into the White Hart Court.
- Invite Aderyn, Vane, or hesitant nobles here for a controlled confrontation.

## Failure and escalation

If discovered, Caddoc first attempts to contain the matter as a ritual dispute. He may lock the chapel, summon Aderyn, or demand that Captain Vane witness the ring before Mael sees it. If the crew damages memorials, threatens witnesses, or handles the ring carelessly, he turns against them. If Mael learns the ring is authentic, he orders the chapel sealed and advances the Great Muster to the earliest moment the bands can be opened.

Use the chapel as route, archive, recruitment scene, or temporary tribunal. Branoc's answer lies below; here the crew learns the grammar and names the cost.

## Custody before House Taran

Behind the lowest memorial board, Caddoc keeps the cauldron's carrying calendar. Nine hearth marks repeat in a circuit: Mere, Ash, Rowan, Gorse, Reed, Stone, Bell, Road, and Lamp. No keeper held the vessel for more than one winter, and questions concerning war, inheritance, or a keeper's own house required three disinterested hearths to witness the first wording. House Taran's emergency writ interrupted the circuit fifty-three years ago. The record contains renewals of the emergency but no release by the surviving hearths.

The same chest defines black-water testimony. A complete Asking produces three exact leaves marked by the bands present and the dead person's free departure. One leaf with two named witnesses stays an oath founded on a contrary recital. Three establish a durable record; living judgment still decides consequence.
